title: Rabia's torch and bucket
hookLine: Rabia of Basra carries fire to burn paradise and water to drown hell, so God is loved for God alone (Attar, Memorial of the Saints)

lines: A WOMAN IN THE STREETS OF BASRA.
cards: A woman is hurrying through the streets of Basra, in what's now Iraq. In one hand, a burning torch. In the other, a bucket of water, sloshing as she goes.
People stop and stare. Finally someone asks the obvious question: where are you going with those? Her answer is still told.
It opens a new week of homes: Sufi teachers, desert monks, and the Buddha.

teach.h: RABIA OF BASRA, AN EARLY SUFI.
teach.b: Rabia al-Adawiyya of Basra is remembered among the early Sufis, the teachers of the inner, mystical path within Islam.

Most of what we know comes from writers who lived long after her, especially the Persian poet Attar, in his Memorial of the Saints. So these are stories told about her, and scholars read them that way.
Tradition says she was born poor, sold into slavery as a girl, and set free after her master saw her praying through the night.
When people ask what the torch and bucket are for, she says, as the story is told: I'm going to set fire to paradise and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both are gone.

teach.h: NO FEAR, NO REWARD — GOD ALONE.
teach.b: Then people will worship God not out of fear of punishment, not out of hope for a reward, but for God alone. It's meant to startle. Rabia isn't mocking heaven or hell; she's asking what's underneath our reasons.

If the reward vanished, and the threat vanished, would the love still be there? Another saying people attribute to her makes the same point: she wanted to love God for God's own beauty, not as a bargain.
You don't have to share her faith to feel the edge of that question. So much of what we do comes with a receipt attached: the praise, the payback, the good review. But there's another kind.
A parent rocking a baby at three in the morning.
Someone singing alone in the car. Nobody's keeping score. That's the love Rabia was walking through Basra for.

how: Sufis honor Rabia al-Adawiyya as an early teacher of love for God for God's own sake, and her story and sayings are told in Sufi gatherings and books of saints.

o: an early Sufi woman of Basra, known for love of God
a Greek doctor who wrote about herbs and fevers
a queen of Basra famed for her gifts to the poor

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: to put out the fires of hell

s: Rabia's story was written down by people who knew her
most of it comes from later writers, like Attar, long after her time.
Rabia was mocking heaven and hell
she was asking whether love for God would remain with no reward and no threat.
tradition says she was once enslaved
the stories say she was sold as a girl and later set free.

games.q: you're in the street in Basra. a woman hurries past with a torch and a bucket of water. you ask what they're for. what does she say?
o: to light the lamps and wash the mosque floor
to burn paradise and put out hell
to cook for the poor of the city
games.why: to burn paradise and put out hell, so that people worship God not from fear or for reward, but for God alone.

practice: Think of something good you did recently, and notice honestly what you hoped to get back: thanks, a good impression, a favor later, with no blame.
Then picture one small good thing you could do that nobody will ever know about, picture no one noticing, and see how that feels. If you pray, you might simply sit with Rabia's question in silence.

wordCard.voice: Rabia. An early Sufi teacher who carried fire for paradise and water for hell, so that what was left was love for its own sake.

orig.note: Arabic: "the fourth." tradition says Rabia was the fourth daughter of her family.

carryVoice: Your line: for its own sake. What's left, with no reward and no threat, is love. See you tomorrow.
